case_name: Taylor et al. v. Despard et al.
text:
Taylor et al. v. Despard et al.

[1956] O.R. 963

ONTARIO

Court of Appeal

Roach, Aylesworth and Schroeder JJ.A.

October 31, 1956.

Defamation -- Qualified Privilege -- Whether Privilege Established -- Mutual Interest -- Express Malice -- Presumption of Absence of Malice -- Whether Words such that Malice can be Inferred.
If the buyer of an automobile from a dealer approaches a finance company for a loan, to be secured by a chattel mortgage on the car, for the purpose of financing the purchase, the company, in the conduct of its own affairs, has an interest in communicating to the buyer its reasons for rejecting his application, and the buyer has an interest in learning those reasons.  Further, both parties have an interest in the title they would acquire in the car, as buyer and mortgagee respectively, if the transaction were completed.  If, therefore, the employee of the finance company, in rejecting the application, makes statements as to the character and reputation of the dealer from whom the applicant is proposing to buy, the occasion is one of qualified privilege, and the dealer cannot succeed in an action for damages for slander unless he proves that the words were spoken maliciously.  Adam v. Ward,
[1917] A.C. 309 at 334,
quoted and applied.
The words "express malice" are words of legal distinction differentiating between the malice that the law implies from the mere publication of defamatory words and the malice that must be proved where, by reason of the occasion being one of qualified privilege, the presumption of malice is rebutted.
Evidence of express malice may be either extrinsic or intrinsic.  Extrinsic evidence consists of evidence, apart from the statements themselves, tending to show that the defendat, in making them, was actuated by personal ill-will or some other improper motive, in contrast to a motive inspired by a sense of duty or the mutual interest created by the occasion.  Intrinsic evidence, on the other hand, is the evidence provided by the words themselves.  Wright v. Woodgate (1835), 2 Cr. M. & R. 573, quoted and applied.  The burden on the plaintiff may be discharged by showing, (1) that the defendant did not himself believe the statements he made, or (2) that in the circumstances known to the defendant it would have been unreasonable for him to believe them, or (3) that the statements were so disproportionate to the occasion as to provide evidence in themselves that the defendant was using the occasion for an improper purpose.  Spill v. Maule (1869), L.R. 4 Exch. 232 at 235-6; Adam v. Ward, supra, at pp. 334 et seq., quoted and applied.
AN APPEAL by the plaintiff from the judgment of Moorhouse J., dismissing an action for damages for slander.
13th and 14th September 1956.  The appeal was heard by ROACH, AYLESWORTH and SCHROEDER JJ.A.
B. Grossberg, Q.C. for the plaintiff, appellant:  I have three submissions to make:  (1) the occasions on which the defamatory words were spoken were not privileged, because (a) the statements went beyond the limitations of duty or interest, (b) the range of the comments was too wide, and (c) the statements were unreasonable; (2) there was ample evidence of malice, which should have been left to the jury; (3) the learned trial judge should have left to the jury the question whether the privilege (assuming that it existed) was exceeded.
There are two lines of cases.  It has been held in one line that excess of language destroys the privilege, and in the other line that excess of language is evidence of malice.
The plaintiff and the defendant did not know each other personally.  The plaintiff had had only one transaction with the defendant company.  There is nothing in the evidence to indicate any basis whatever for the statements made by Despard; all that he had to say to explain his actions was, "We will not deal with Taylor."  In either view, whether the excess destroys the privilege or is evidence of malice, the issue should have been left to the jury.
On the question of qualified privilege I should like to cite Tuson v. Evans
(1840), 12 Ad. & El. 733 at 736, 113 E.R. 991
; Lawrence v. Finch,
1930 CanLII 431 (ON SCAD)
, 66 O.L.R. 451, [1931] 1 D.L.R. 689.  Cases that hold that a qualified privilege is destroyed by excessive language are: Halls v. Mitchell,
1928 CanLII 1 (SCC)
, [1928] S.C.R. 125, [1928] 2 D.L.R. 97; Graham v. Crozier (1897), 44 U.C.Q.B. 378; Fryer v. Kinnersley
(1863), 15 C.B.N.S. 422, 143 E.R. 849
; Quillinan v. Stuart (1917),
1917 CanLII 512 (ON SCAD)
, 38 O.L.R. 623 at 635, 35 D.L.R. 35; Winstanley v. Bampton,
[1943] K.B. 319, [1943] 1 All E.R. 661
; Arnott v. The College of Physicians and Surgeons of the Province of Saskatchewan,
1954 CanLII 60 (SCC)
, [1954] S.C.R. 538 at 551, [1955] 1 D.L.R. 1; Watt v. Longsdon,
[1930] 1 K.B. 130 at 142,
154.  It is not necessary to reconcile the two lines of cases.  If there is evidence either that the privilege was exceeded or that there was malice, it must go to the jury.
[ROACH J.A.:  Do you distinguish between the defendant Despard and the defendant company? The words were spoken in the course of Despard's employment, but does slander come within the scope of employment?]  The defendant company must be liable for the acts of its employees.
J.J. Robinette, Q.C., for the defendants, respondents:  I submit, as was submitted at trial, that the words were spoken on occasions of qualified privilege, and that there was no evidence of malice to go to the jury.  Each occasion must be considered in itself:  20 Halsbury, 2nd ed. 1936, p. 474; C. v. D.,
1924 CanLII 456 (BC SC)
, 56 O.L.R. 209, 506, [1925] 1 D.L.R. 734, 43 C.C.C. 235. As to malice, I rely on Adam v. Ward,
[1917] A.C. 309
; Knapp v. McLeod,
1926 CanLII 374 (ON SCAD)
, 58 O.L.R. 605 at 606, 611, [1926] 2 D.L.R. 1083.
All the statements were made in reference to business dealings and so long as the language used was relevant the privilege was not lost.  Once it is established that an occasion is one of qualified privilege, the truth of the statements is presumed, as is the bona fides of the speaker, and even if the plaintiff proves that the statements were untrue that of itself will not destroy the privilege, nor is it evidence of malice.  To constitute malice within the meaning of the authorities there must be personal spite.
[AYLESWORTH J.A.:  Can malice not be inferred from the words themselves?]  Not from the words proved in this case:  Gatley on Libel and Slander, 4th ed. 1953, pp. 282-3, s. 5; p. 284; Jenoure v. Delmege,
[1891] A.C. 73 at 79
; Todd v. Dun, Wiman & Co. et al.
(1888), 15 O.A.R. 85
; Ross v. Bucke
(1892), 21 O.R. 692
; Laughton v. The Bishop of Sodor and Man (1872), L.R. 4 P.C. 495; Turner (otherwise Robertson) v. Metro-Goldwyn-Mayor Pictures Ltd.
[1950] 1 All E.R. 449 at 455
.
Even if Despard might be held liable, the defendant company could not be.
We are dealing with several causes of action, and the question of qualified privilege must be considered in connection with each one of them:  Adam v. Ward, supra, at p. 339.
B. Grossberg, Q.C., in reply:  A case is authority only in respect of its particular facts, and I suggest that Jenoure v. Delmege, supra, is not binding on this Court.
Gatley, op. cit., 3rd ed. 1938, at p. 436, suggests that a master will be liable for slander spoken by his servant.
Cur. adv. vult.
31st October 1956.  The judgment of the Court was delivered by

B. Grossberg, Q.C., for the plaintiff, appellant.
J.J. Robinette, Q.C., for the defendants, respondents.

ROACH J.A.:-- This is an appeal by the plaintiffs from the
judgment pronounced by Mr. Justice Moorhouse and dated 20th
March 1956, dismissing the plaintiffs' action with costs.  The
plaintiff Walter Taylor at the relevant times was in the
business of buying and selling motor cars in the city of
Sudbury.  His co-plaintiff was also engaged in that business
and he was its president.

The defendant corporation was engaged in the business of
financing the purchase of motor cars by lending money to the
purchasers on the security of chattel mortgages thereon.  At
all relevant times the defendant Despard was the assistant
branch manager of that company in the city of Sudbury.

The plaintiffs' claim is for damages for slander.  The
plaintiffs pleaded that the defendant Despard in the course of
and while acting within the scope of his employment, published
oral defamatory statements of and concerning the plaintiffs to
three persons, by name Henry Lachance, Heinz Boy and Frederick
Franklyn.

I.  With respect to the statements made to Lachance the
plaintiffs specifically pleaded:

(i)  That in the month of April or May 1955 Despard made the
following statements to him:

"'Mr. Taylor is very shady'

"'He is a crooked car dealer'

"'He buys and sells cars that are not his to sell'

"'One fellow pretty nearly lost his shirt in a deal with
Taylor and Union Acceptance Corporation Limited had to
eventually take the car and resell it and the Purchaser from
Taylor had been left with nothing', and the Defendant, Despard,
meant ... thereby that the Plaintiffs were guilty of
fraudulent, corrupt and dishonest practices in their trade.

"'No finance company is going to touch Taylor's transactions'
and the Defendant, Despard, meant ... thereby that it was
because the Plaintiffs were untrustworthy, fraudulent and
corrupt in their said trade.'

"(ii) And in a subsequent conversation about two weeks later
in April or May, 1955, [Despard made the following statement to
him]:

"'Mr. Taylor is disreputable and a fraud'

"'Mr. Taylor is the North's most crooked dealer'";

(iii) and that later, namely on or about 15th July 1955,
Despard spoke words of and concerning the plaintiffs, the
plaintiffs being unaware of the exact language, but that the
words were to the effect that the plaintiff Taylor had gone
bankrupt.

II.  With respect to the statements made to Heinz Boy the
plaintiffs pleaded:

(i)  that on or about 3rd June 1955 Despard made a statement
to him in language of the exact words of which the plaintiffs
are unaware, but which was to the effect that the plaintiff
Taylor and his co-plaintiff "were dishonest and not worthy of
the trust of the said Heinz Boy in dealings involving the
purchase by him of an automobile from the Plaintiff Company";

(ii) that at the same time Despard made a statement to Boy in
language of the exact words of which the plaintiffs are
unaware, but which was "to the effect that some person whose
identity is unknown to the Plaintiffs or to the said Heinz Boy,
had purchased a Lincoln automobile from the Plaintiff Company
and had been forced to surrender it because the Plaintiff
Taylor had not paid for it at the place where he obtained it,
and the Defendant, Despard, meant thereby that the Plaintiffs
were guilty of fraudulent, corrupt and dishonest practices in
their said trade, or in the alternative he meant that the
plaintiffs were in insolvent circumstances and were not able to
meet their obligations as they fell due";

(iii) that at the same time Despard made a statement to him
in language of the exact words of which the plaintiffs are
unaware but which was "to the effect that the Plaintiff Taylor
had been bankrupt in Timmins, Ontario, and because he had been
bankrupt he had changed his name to Taylor".

III. With respect to the statements alleged to have been made
to Frederick Franklyn the plaintiffs specifically pleaded that
on 16th or 17th June 1955:

(i) Despard made this statement to him, namely:

"'Some of our best customers have lost a lot of money as a
result of dealing with Mr. Taylor', and the Defendant, Despard,
meant thereby that persons unknown to the Plaintiff, Taylor,
had suffered loss by reason of the dishonesty of Taylor, or
that the Plaintiff, Taylor, was guilty of sharp business
practices in dealing with the said people, or that he was in
insolvent circumstances and not able to meet his obligations as
they fell due.

"'Several people tried to recover their money from Mr.
Taylor, but Mr. Taylor knew the ropes and they could not get
anywhere with him', and the Defendant, Despard, meant thereby
that several people were unable to recover their money because
of Taylor's dishonest, fraudulent and corrupt practices, or in
the alternative he meant that several people were unable to
recover their monies because the plaintiff Taylor was
unreliable and not a man of his word or that he indulged in
sharp and unconscionable business practises";

(ii) that at the same time Despard made a statement to him in
language of the exact words of which the plaintiffs are
unaware, but which was "to the effect that in some cases when
the Defendant Corporation had financed the sales of the
Plaintiffs' cars and money had been paid over to the Plaintiff
Taylor, the Plaintiff Taylor did not pay it over to the dealers
from whom he bargained to purchase the automobiles which were
the subject of the same transaction in which the Defendant
Corporation was a party with the result that in those cases the
unpaid dealers repossessed the cars and the persons who had
bought the cars in these transactions lost their money due to
the fault of and the dishonesty of the Plaintiff Taylor";

(iii) that at the same time Despard made a statement to him
in language of the exact words of which the plaintiffs are
unaware, but which was "to the effect that the Plaintiff Taylor
was guilty of sharp business practises, and the Defendant
Despard, meant thereby that the Plaintiff Taylor was guilty of
fraudulent, corrupt and dishonest practices in his said trade";

(iv)  that at the same time Despard made a statement to him
in language of the exact words of which the plaintiffs are
unaware, but which was "to the effect that the Plaintiff Taylor
had gone bankrupt in Timmins, Ontario, and in order to avoid
the consequences of bankruptcy he had changed his name";

(v) that at the same time Despard made a statement to him in
language of the exact words of which the plaintiffs are
unaware, but which was "to the effect that the Plaintiff Taylor
had changed his name in order to escape his creditors";

(vi) that at the same time Despard made a statement to him in
language of the exact words of which the plaintiffs are
unaware, but which was "to the effect that the Plaintiff Taylor
Distributing Company Limited did not stand up to its promises,
and the Defendant, Despard, meant thereby that the Plaintiff
Company was untrustworthy and unreliable, and that the said
Frederick Franklyn ought not therefor [sic] to deal with it";

(vii) that at the same time Despard made a statement to him
in language of the exact words of which the plaintiffs are
unaware, but which was "to the effect that the Defendant, Union
Acceptance Corporation Limited had tried to repossess a 1954
Lincoln automobile which the Plaintiff Corporation and the
Plaintiff Taylor acting as its agent had sold and the sale of
which it had financed and when they tried to so repossess it
the Plaintiff Taylor hid the car, and the Defendant, Despard,
meant thereby that the plaintiff Taylor did so without colour
of right and in so doing was guilty of fraudulent, corrupt and
dishonest practises in the way of his said trade, and he
further meant that the Plaintiff Corporation recognized and
adopted the plaintiff Taylor's actions";

(viii) that at the same time Despard made a statement to him
in language of the exact words of which the plaintiffs are
unaware, but which was "to the effect that no company in
Sudbury would finance any of the Plaintiff Corporation's
transactions involving the sale of cars and the Defendant,
Despard, meant thereby that the Plaintiff Corporation was
guilty of fraudulent, corrupt and dishonest practices in its
said trade";

(ix) that at the same time Despard made a statement to him in
language of the exact words of which the plaintiffs are
unaware, but which was "to the effect that the Plaintiff Taylor
was untrustworthy";

(x) that at the same time Despard made a statement to him in
language of the exact words of which the plaintiffs are
unaware, but which was "to the effect that the Plaintiff Taylor
cleverly avoided criminal prosecutions, but sooner or later the
law would catch up to him, and the Defendant, Despard, meant
thereby that the Plaintiff Taylor customarily and frequently
broke the law and was therefore a corrupt and dishonest
person".

The defendants in their pleading denied the publication
alleged and also pleaded that if the statements were published
they were published on occasions of qualified privilege and
that in so publishing them the defendants were not actuated by
any malice.

At the close of the plaintiffs' case, on motion by counsel
for the defendants, the learned trial judge granted a nonsuit.
He held that the statements were published on occasions of
qualified privilege and that there was no evidence of malice to
go to the jury.  Having so held he withdrew the case from the
jury and granted judgment dismissing the action with costs.

The evidence of Lachance was as follows:

At the relevant times this witness was in the business of
selling new and used cars.  Sometimes he sold independent of
Walter Taylor and sometimes either as an agent for or in co-
operation with Walter Taylor.  In April or May 1955 this
witness was attempting to promote the sale of a number of motor
cars to be used as taxi-cabs in and around the city of Sudbury
and in connection with this prospect he interviewed the
defendant Despard to ascertain whether or not Union Acceptance
Corporation would finance the prospective purchasers.  During
this discussion Despard brought up the name of Mr. Taylor and
"he said Mr. Taylor was a shady dealer, he was a crooked
dealer and no other finance company would touch him ... and if
I had anything to do with him they wouldn't touch me either".

Two or three weeks later in connection with another
prospective sale, this witness again spoke to the defendant
Despard and Despard told him "not to have anything to do with
Mr. Taylor" that he "was one of the North's most crooked
dealers; that he bought cars and sold cars that weren't his to
sell".

The evidence of Heinz Boy was as follows:

In late May or early June 1955, he wanted to buy a motor car
and was referred by a friend to the plaintiff Walter Taylor.
As a result of discussions with Taylor he agreed to purchase a
motor car from him and gave him a cheque for $300 as a deposit.
He then went to the office of the corporate defendant for the
purpose of arranging a loan.  There he met the defendant
Despard and told him that he wanted to borrow $500 or $600 to
enable him to pay the balance of the purchase-price; of the
full balance he was short that amount.  Despard inquired from
whom he was purchasing the car and Boy replied that he was
purchasing it from Walter Taylor.  Despard then said "he was
sorry he could not finance the car for me.  He wouldn't finance
anything for him."  I should here interpose that Heinz Boy is a
German immigrant.  He understands the English language but has
a limited capacity to speak it.  Notwithstanding that limited
capacity he gave his evidence in the English language and I
quote from it:

"He [Despard] told me he [Walter Taylor] was dishonest and,
like, if you want to call it untrustworthy whatever it is, and
I shouldn't deal with him.  I should deal with more or less a
reliable dealer, something like that.  And he gave me an
example of a fellow who bought a Lincoln. I don't know what
year it was.  He gave me an example of that fellow who bought a
Lincoln and lost his car, the Lincoln, and everything, they
took it away on him because, I don't know, there was a lien or
something against the car which wasn't paid off some place
... that is the example he gave me.  And that is why they
wouldn't finance anything for him.  The other fellow bought a
car off Walter Taylor and that car wasn't supposed to be paid
off or something like that and there was a lien against it or
something.  I don't remember to recall the exact words any more
that he used at the time ... that he [Walter Taylor] had
changed his name to Taylor for some reason ... that he changed
his name and he was a Jew."

The evidence of Frederick Franklyn was as follows:

In May or early June 1955 this witness, desiring to purchase
a motor car, discussed a possible purchase with a number of
dealers in motor cars in Sudbury and decided to accept the
proposal submitted to him by the plaintiff Walter Taylor.  It
was necessary for this witness, too, to borrow money on the
security of the car to pay part of the purchase-price and for
that purpose he went to the office of the defendant corporation
and there he met the defendant Despard. After some preliminary
discussion Despard asked him from whom he was going to buy it
and the witness said "from Mr. Taylor".  Despard then advised
him "not to buy a car from Taylor" and the witness asked
Despard why he should not buy from Taylor and Despard gave the
witness several reasons.  For one, "he said he would not advise
me to buy from Mr. Taylor because some of the Union Finance
customers had lost a lot of money through dealing with Mr.
Taylor".  The witness then asked Despard why they lost money
and Despard replied:  "In certain cases they [meaning Union
Acceptance Corporation] had financed some of Mr. Taylor's deals
in the past and Mr. Taylor had failed to pay over the money
they had paid him to the dealer concerned where he got the car
from and the customers eventually lost their money and the cars
because they were repossessed, because the money never reached
the dealer ..."  "He said people tried to get the money back
from Mr. Taylor but they couldn't get anywhere at all with him
because he knew all the ropes, I mean he always knew his way
out they just lost their money."  He "advised me to buy the car
from a reputable dealer like Gardiners because he said at least
I could rely on their word to stand up to their promises".
"Another thing he said, Mr. Taylor had gone bankrupt up
north in Timmins, I think, and had to leave in a hurry because
creditors were after him. Also said something about him
changing his name in order to avoid the bankruptcy."  "He
represented that I would be far better off to deal with a
reputable dealer because one couldn't trust Taylor he wasn't
very honest and I might lose money if I deal with him."

This witness then inquired from Despard how it would be
possible for a man like this to operate.  Despard replied "that
Mr. Taylor was very clever but sooner or later the law will
catch up with him".

In my opinion the learned trial judge was right in holding
that all the occasions upon which Despard made the statements
of and concerning Walter Taylor to those three persons were
occasions of qualified privilege.

".... a privileged occasion is, in reference to qualified
privilege, an occasion where the person who makes a
communication has an interest or a duty, legal, social, or
moral, to make it to the person to whom it is made, and the
person to whom it is so made has a corresponding interest or
duty to receive it.  This reciprocity is essential."  Per Lord
Atkinson in Adam v. Ward,
[1917] A.C. 309 at 334
.

Union Acceptance Corporation Limited in the conduct of its
own affairs had an interest in communicating to each of those
three persons its reasons for rejecting applications for loans
on the security of motor cars purchased from Walter Taylor and
each of those three persons, as such applicants, had an
interest in learning those reasons.  Moreover, that company and
each of those persons had a vital interest in the title they
would respectively acquire in the motor car, those persons as
purchasers, the company as chattel mortgagee.  In the ordinary
course of business the company could speak to prospective or
actual customers only through its officers or employees.
Despard as one of its employees was entitled to whatever
protection the privileged occasion gave to his employer.

It was conceded by counsel for the plaintiffs that if these
were occasions of qualified privilege no action lay for the
publication of the statements complained of unless they were
made maliciously and that the burden rested on the plaintiff
Walter Taylor to prove express malice.  Whether or not Despard
was actuated by malice would be a question of fact for the jury
to decide; but whether or not there was any evidence of malice
to go to the jury was a question of law for the trial judge to
decide.

"Express malice" are words of legal distinction
differentiating between malice which the law implies from the
mere publication of defamatory words and the malice which must
be proved where, by reason of the occasion being one of
qualified privilege, the presumption of malice is thereby
rebutted.

Evidence of express malice may be extrinsic or intrinsic.
Extrinsic evidence consists of evidence apart from the
statements themselves that tends to show that in publishing the
statement the defendant was actuated by a motive of personal
ill-will or some other improper motive in contrast to a motive
inspired by a sense of duty or the mutual interest which the
occasion created.  Intrinsic evidence is that evidence which
the words themselves provide.

In Wright v. Woodgate
(1835), 2 Cr. M. & R. 573, 150 E.R.
244
, Parke B. dealt with that question thus:  "In the present
case it became, in my opinion, encumbent upon the plaintiff to
shew malice in fact.  This he might have made out, either from
the language of the letter itself, or by extrinsic evidence, as
by proof of the conduct or expressions of the defendant,
shewing that he was actuated by a motive of personal ill-will."

In this case there was no extrinsic evidence of malice but it
was submitted by counsel for the appellants that in the very
nature and quality of the words themselves, after giving due
regard to the occasions on which they were spoken, there was
sufficient evidence of malice to require the trial judge to
allow the case to go to the jury.

It must be kept in mind that the truth or falsity of the
statements complained of is not in issue.  For the purposes of
the trial they are regarded as being false.

Since each of the statements was made on an occasion of
qualified privilege, then, apart, of course, from the issue as
to whether or not the words were spoken, the only other matter
in issue was the bona fides of the defendants.  That bona fides
in the circumstances is presumed.  The burden was on the
plaintiffs to rebut that presumption.

It was not for the trial judge to say whether or not that
presumption was rebutted.  That would be a matter for the jury
to decide.  The trial judge's duty was to determine whether or
not there was any evidence adduced by the plaintiffs tending to
show lack of good faith, that is, malice. On the motion for
nonsuit the learned trial judge had to address himself to these
questions and on this appeal this Court must address itself to
them, namely:  First, was there any evidence tending to show
that the defendant Despard did not believe the statements that
he made?  If there was then the trial judge should have let the
case go to the jury.  Secondly, if there was no such evidence
then was there evidence tending to show that in the
circumstances known to Despard it would be unreasonable that he
should believe the statements to be true?  If there was
evidence tending to show that fact, then the trial judge should
have let the case go to the jury.  Thirdly, if there was no
evidence tending to show that the defendant did not belive the
statements to be true and that in the circumstances known to
him it would be unreasonable for him so to believe, then were
the statements so disproportionate to the occasion as to
provide evidence that the defendant was using the occasion for
an improper purpose?  If the language used was capable of that
interpretation, then the trial judge should have let the case
go to the jury so they could decide that question.

Before addressing myself to these questions it may be
appropriate to refer to certain authorities.

The first is Spill v. Maule (1869), L.R. 4 Exch. 232.  There
Cockburn C.J. at pp. 235-6 said this:  'We are all agreed that
the general proposition contended for by the counsel for the
plaintiff is right, and that it may be that the language used
in a libel, though under other circumstances justifiable, may
be so much too violent for the occasion and circumstances to
which it is applied, as to form strong evidence of malice, upon
the issue of whether the communication is covered by the
privilege, and that an inference of actual malice may be drawn
from its use.  If, therefore, any question of fact arose with
respect to the circumstances, it should be left to the jury.
But we must look to see what really took place on this
occasion."

Then having outlined what did take place, as to which there
was no dispute, the learned Chief Justice continued:  "The
question then arises, whether the language is too strong for
the occasion; the terms applied to the plaintiff's conduct
being 'most disgraceful and dishonest.'  Now, the communication
being privileged, the presumption is in favour of the absence
of malice in the defendant, and in order to rebut this
presumption, the plaintiff must show actual malice, and he may
no doubt show this by a reference to the terms of the libel as
being utterly beyond and disproportionate to the facts.  We
must look, then, to see whether the circumstances are such as
to rebut on the part of the plaintiff the presumption of the
absence of malice in the defendant."

The Chief Justice then analyzed the circumstances which were
as he put it "capable of two-fold construction", one that the
plaintiff "could not properly be exposed to any moral censure",
the other that he acted "dishonestly and disgracefully"; and he
stated that because of the presumption of innocence in his
favour it had to be assumed that the defendant did entertain
that view of the plaintiff's acts which induced him to believe,
and honestly to believe and say, that the plaintiff's conduct
was dishonest and disgraceful.

Then follows language in which the Chief Justice embodied the
rule.  He said:  "We have not to deal with the question whether
the plaintiff did or did not act dishonestly and disgracefully;
all we have to examine is whether the defendant stated no more
than what he believed, and what he might reasonably believe; if
he stated no more than this, he is not liable, and, unless
proof to the contrary is produced, we must take it that he did
state no more."

It is of first importance to appreciate that the Chief
Justice laid down two requirements to the immunity of the
defendant from liability.  First, that he believed the
statement was true; secondly, that it was not unreasonable that
he should so believe.  Those requirements must co-exist.
Having regard to the presumption of good faith the burden rests
on the plaintiff in the first instance to adduce evidence
tending to show that the defendant did not believe the
statement to be true, or, if he believed it was true, then that
it was unreasonable for him so to believe because there was no
reasonable foundation for such belief.

Supposing that the plaintiff fails to meet that burden, then
what is the result?  The inquiry does not end there.  The
position of the defendant at that stage is simply this, namely,
the presumption in his favour stands; he is presumed to have
believed the statements to be true and it is presumed that
having regard to the circumstances it was not unreasonable that
he should so believe.  The Court then moves on to the next
consideration, namely, notwithstanding that belief, is the
language of the statement so violent and disproportionate to
the occasion as to provide evidence of malice?

In Adam v. Ward supra, Lord Atkinson at pp. 334 et seq.,
dealing with the question of the quality of the language used
on an occasion of qualified privilege, said this:  "It was,
however, strenuously contended on the part of the appellant, as
I understand, that the language used in a communication made on
a privileged occasion must, if it is to be protected, merely be
such as is reasonably necessary to enable the party making it
to protect the interest or discharge the duty upon which the
qualified privilege is founded.  It has long been established
by unquestioned and unquestionable authority, I think, that
this is not the law."

He then referred to Spill v. Maule, supra.  Having quoted
what Chief Justice Cockburn there said, Lord Atkinson said:  "I
cannot find that the authority of this case has ever been
questioned.  It was cited with approval in the case of Laughton
v. Bishop of Sodor and Man, L.R. 4 P.C. 495 to which I am about
to refer.  It will be observed that the Chief Justice says that
the terms of the libel which are evidence of malice are not
merely such as are beyond the necessities of the occasion, but
such as are utterly beyond and disproportionate to the facts."

Then Lord Atkinson referred to Laughton v. The Bishop of
Sodor and Man, supra and quoted with approval what was there
said, namely:  "Some expressions here used" (i.e., used by the
defendant in his defence) "undoubtedly go beyond what was
necessary for self-defence, but it does not, therefore, follow
that they afford evidence of malice for a jury.  To submit the
language of privileged communications to a strict scrutiny, and
to hold all excess beyond the absolute exigency of the occasion
to be evidence of malice, would in effect greatly limit, if not
altogether defeat, the protection which the law throws over
privileged communications."

Next Lord Atkinson referred to Nevill v. The fine Art and
General Insurance Company, Limited,
[1897] A.C. 68
, and he
distilled the rule from those three authorities to be as
follows, at p. 339:

"These authorities, in my view, clearly establish that a
person making a communication on a privileged occasion is not
restricted to the use of such language merely as is reasonably
necessary to protect the interest or discharge the duty which
is the foundation of his privilege; but that, on the contrary,
he will be protected, even though his language should be
violent or excessively strong, if, having regard to all the
circumstances of the case, he might have honestly and on
reasonable grounds believed that what he wrote or said was true
and necessary for the purpose of his vindication."

In that same case Finlay L.C. at p. 318 said:  "It is further
for the judge to decide whether there is any evidence of
express malice fit to be left to the jury -- that is, whether
there is any evidence on which a reasonable man could find
malice."

The law is well settled that in order to enable a plaintiff
to have the question of malice submitted to the jury -- and I
am of course dealing only with occasions of qualified privilege
-- it is necessary that the evidence should raise a probability
of malice and be more consistent with its existence than with
its non-existence and that there must be more than a mere
scintilla of evidence.

In addressing myself to the three questions which the learned
trial judge had to consider and which this Court must now
consider, I must of course examine the evidence and see what
the circumstances were.

In addition to the three persons to whom the three statements
were made, Taylor was the only other witness on behalf of the
plaintiffs.  The following is a summary of his evidence:

His name was originally Walter Finkleman.  He was born in
Englehart in Northern Ontario, and in 1937 he went into the
business of buying and selling motor cars in the town of
Timmins. There he carried on that business under the name of
Moneta Motors.  In 1948 he caused Taylor Distributing Company
Limited to be incorporated.  The other shareholders of that
company were, and apparently still are, his father Hyman
Finkleman, his wife Doris Taylor, and his two daughters Sheila
and Rosalie.  The evidence is a bit confusing but as I
understand it, that company dealt in petroleum products and
Taylor himself carried on the business of buying and selling
motor cars, as I earlier said, under the name of Moneta Motors.
The business of Moneta Motors continued until early 1953.  By
that time, and indeed earlier, as will appear from something
Taylor said in evidence and to which I shall refer in a moment,
Taylor was hopelessly insolvent:  he owed about $80,000.  His
principal creditors were Canadian Acceptance Corporation
Limited and the Bank of Nova Scotia.  He owed the former
$47,000 and the latter about $30,000.  "A lot of people", so he
said, sued him and got judgment.  In 1953 he "wound up" the
business of Moneta Motors "as best [he] could". I do not know
what his "best" was.  At one place in his evidence he speaks of
having sold it out and at another place of having wound it up
and, indeed, in another place of its still being carried on.
In 1951 he became ill and stated in evidence that he "found out
[he] had cancer".  He made a number of trips to the Mayo
Clinic in the United States.  In 1951, being the year when he
said he discovered he had cancer, he took up residence in the
city of Hamilton where apparently, notwithstanding that he was
suffering from cancer, he started "looking around for either a
service-station or a used car lot because [he] could see the
writing on the wall that [he] was going to be finished in
Timmins eventually".  I have difficulty in reconciling the
reason that he gave for choosing Hamilton in preference to
Timmins and deciding to launch a new business in Hamilton when
he already had one in Timmins.  There is probably more truth
than fiction in what he said about being "finished in Timmins
eventually" and he was probably taking time by the forelock and
getting out of there.  In his evidence he said he preferred the
north country because he regarded himself as "a northerner".
Notwithstanding that preference, and in the circumstances that
I have related, he took up residence in Hamilton and Moneta
Motors continued to operate in Timmins until, as he says, he
either sold it out or wound it up or something happened to it
which is very indefinite, in 1953.  He remained in Hamilton
until late in 1953 and while in Hamilton he carried on the
business of buying and selling motor cars from his residence
there.  In August 1953, while still living in Hamilton, he had
his name legally changed to Taylor.  In the fall of 1953
-- that would be after he changed his name -- he moved to
Oakville notwithstanding that according to him he still
preferred the north country.  He remained in Oakville only a
few months during which time he there carried on the business
of buying and selling cars from his residence.  In December
1953 he went on a visit to Sudbury and he moved to Sudbury
early in 1954 or it may have been in December 1953 -- the
evidence is a bit vague.  In Sudbury he obtained employment as
service-manager in a garage known as Duncan Motors and
continued in that job until February 1955.  While so employed,
and with the approval of his employer, he bought and sold cars
in his free time.  His employment with Duncan Motors terminated
at the end of January 1955, and from then until this action was
started he devoted his whole time to the business of buying and
selling cars.

In considering the evidence I must say that from time to time
I almost lost track of the corporate plaintiff because on page
after page of the evidence it seems to be plain that Taylor
himself was carrying on the business, then suddenly a question
is interjected as to the profits being made by the company.
Certainly nowhere in the evidence does the plaintiff Taylor
make it plain that it was the corporate plaintiff that was
carrying on the business and that he was only its servant or
officer.

Taylor's business dealings with Union Acceptance Corporation
Limited commenced when he was carrying on business in Timmins.
This is the way he put it in evidence:  "I dealt with their
agent in Timmins and financed my cars personally with them in
Toronto."

During his period of employment with Duncan Motors he sold,
by his own estimate, 20 to 25 cars, but he had dealings with
Union Acceptance Corporation Limited in respect of only one of
them.  This is the way he put it:  "They bought me out on one
car sold ... in 1954." There is evidence that either in 1954 or
1955, it is not at all clear as to the year, he applied to
Union Acceptance Corporation Limited to finance the purchase of
a car he was selling to a customer and the company refused.
There were other finance companies doing a similar business in
Sudbury but he frankly admitted in evidence he "couldn't get
financing from them".  Neither was he able to arrange financing
with any bank in Sudbury.  Finding himself in that predicament
he made some sort of arrangement with Lachance.  My
understanding of the evidence is that the deals would be put
through in Lachance's name and Lachance would arrange the
financing and for every such deal Taylor paid Lachance $25.
There were about 30 such deals.  Some time in 1955 he applied
to a firm in Toronto, referred to in the evidence as Danforth
Discount, and succeeded in making some arrangement, the details
of which were not disclosed in evidence, whereby that firm
purchased conditional sales agreements covering cars sold by
him.  He also made some arrangements with the Imperial Bank in
Oakville whereby the purchases of some cars sold by him were
financed.  The details of those arrangements were not disclosed
in evidence.

Taylor's father is a man of financial substance and between
father and son they have paid in full the indebtedness to the
Bank of Nova Scotia in Timmins and about $45,000 on the
indebtedness to Canadian Acceptance Corporation.  It does not
appear how much was paid by the father and how much by the son,
or whether the payment by the father was gratuitous or by
virtue of some contractual obligation.  Taylor has still a
number of judgment creditors to whom he is making periodical
payments.

Taylor had never met Despard before this lawsuit was started.

When asked in examination-in-chief if he could give any
reason why the statements complained of in this action should
have been made, his reply was:  "I don't know why anybody I
don't know would knock me like that.  I can't find any reason
at all why he would say these things because I have never said
anything about them."  I fully appreciate that for the purposes
of the trial the statements complained of are to be regarded as
false, but having been asked that question, where was a golden
opportunity for Taylor to say there was no reason that would
justify these defendants making those statements because they
were not true, and that there was no reasonable basis on which
Despard could have believed they were true.  Instead he merely
said that he did not know why anybody who did not know him
would "knock" him like that.  It is not likely that he intended
it to be understood that those who did know him would so
"knock" him. Turning now to the questions which the trial
judge had to ask himself, and which I must ask myself, I answer
the first question in the negative, that is, there was no
evidence tending to show that Despard did not believe that the
statements he made were true.  I answer the second question in
the negative, that is, that there was no evidence tending to
show that it was unreasonable in the circumstances for Despard
to believe that the statements were true.  I answer the third
question by saying that I am not convinced that having regard
to all the circumstances known to Despard, and the omissions
and admissions in Taylor's own evidence, the language used by
Despard in his statements to the three persons who consulted
him were so utterly beyond and disproportionate to the occasion
as to be evidence of malice.  I do not think the language used
raises a probability of malice.  I am not convinced that the
use of the language was more consistent with malice than with
its absence.

I would therefore dismiss the appeal with costs.

Appeal dismissed with costs.
